citations.quote:
Assume the Axiom of Choice. For Jordan curves $C$ and $C'$ in $\mathbb R^2$,
every homeomorphism $h:C\to C'$ extends to a homeomorphism
$H:\mathbb R^2\to\mathbb R^2$ that maps the bounded and unbounded complementary
components of $C$ to the corresponding components of $C'$. In particular each
closed bounded Jordan region is a closed $2$-disk.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. A compact $C^2$ surface, with regular $C^2$ boundary allowed, is $C^2$ diffeomorphic to a compact smooth surface with smooth boundary. For a compact cooriented embedded surface in a smooth three-manifold, the diffeomorphism can be obtained by arbitrarily small local ambient displacements. This also applies to a compact intrinsic subsurface of a $C^2$ leaf: compactness is in the leaf topology, and its boundary is regular in that topology.

A connected oriented closed such surface with Euler characteristic zero is $C^2$ diffeomorphic to $T^2$. A compact regular surface region homeomorphic to a closed disk is $C^2$ diffeomorphic to $D^2$, and any prescribed $C^2$ diffeomorphism of its boundary circle can be realized by the disk parametrization.

Two disjoint regular closed disk regions in a $C^2$ sphere can simultaneously be carried to the standard two disk windows by a $C^2$ diffeomorphism, with compatible prescribed boundary parametrizations. A $C^2$ scalar function defined on a neighborhood of a compact set in $\mathbb R^2$ admits smooth approximations uniformly with its derivatives through order two on that compact set.

Finally let $L$ be a $C^2$ surface and $u:D^2\to L$ an **intrinsically continuous** map which is $C^2$ on an open boundary collar. On any smaller closed boundary collar contained in that open collar, $u$ has arbitrarily close $C^2$ approximations agreeing with $u$ on a neighborhood of the smaller collar, and a homotopy to each approximation fixed there. Closeness is uniform for any fixed compatible metric on $L$. No injectivity or immersion of the cap map is required.

In ZF,

$$\mathrm{AC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{DC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_\omega\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_{\omega,\mathrm{fin}}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_{\omega,2},\qquad \mathrm{AC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_2.$$

DC here includes a prescribed initial point.

derivations.claim: Suppose a circle misses all white disks. By the first hypothesis it lies in $\operatorname{int}Y_i$ for some $i$ and bounds an inside disk there by [F1]. Any other trace circle meeting this disk lies wholly inside it, since trace circles are disjoint. Choose an innermost one among the finitely many contained circles, and call it $\gamma$; write $A$ for its inside disk. Thus $A\cap\Gamma=\gamma$. The circle $\gamma$ meets the core $B_i$: otherwise it lies in a single ear, contradicting the assumption that all intersections with ears are proper arcs. It also cannot lie entirely in $B_i$, by the corresponding proper-arc assumption for the core.

Cut the core disk along all the proper arcs of $\Gamma\cap B_i$. A proper arc in a disk together with either of the two boundary paths is a Jordan curve; [F1] gives its two disk sides. Induction over the finite disjoint arcs therefore makes every resulting region have disk closure, with the smooth corner parameters of [F2]. Because $\operatorname{int}A$ has no trace, each component of $\operatorname{int}A\cap B_i$ is the interior, relative to $B_i$, of one of these regions. Choose one incident to an arc of $\gamma\cap B_i$ on its $A$ side, and denote its closure by $R$. This is an actual disk with corners. Its boundary consists of one or more whole arcs of $\gamma\cap B_i$ and intervals of $\partial B_i$. No other trace circle contributes to $\partial R$, by step1.1. Moreover every interval of $\partial R$ not on $\gamma$ lies in an attaching interval $J_{ij}$: the remaining parts of $\partial B_i$ are in $\partial Y_i$, whereas $A\subset\operatorname{int}Y_i$. The boundary of $R$ contains at least one trace arc by its choice.

If $\partial R$ contains just one trace arc $\beta$, its complementary boundary path lies in the disjoint union of the attaching intervals, hence in a single $J_{ij}\subset\partial B$. The disk $R\subset B$ therefore makes $\beta$ boundary-parallel in $B$, contrary to the second hypothesis. If $\partial R$ contains at least two trace arcs, join interior points on two different such arcs by a smooth embedded arc through $\operatorname{int}R$, using its actual disk parameter. Its interior misses $\Gamma\cup\partial B_i$, and both endpoint arcs belong to $\gamma$. This contradicts the third hypothesis. Both alternatives are impossible. Hence no trace circle misses all white disks.

Each circle therefore contains at least one component arc of the white trace, and disjoint circles contain disjoint such arcs. Counting the finite nonempty sets of arcs on each circle gives $N\leq M$; when $M=0$ this also proves $N=0$. No choice of a representative arc from an infinite family is involved.

Surgery along a chord on one circle has two outcomes obtained by joining the two complementary paths of that circle to the two sides of a thin chord rectangle. Both outcomes are circles, and all other circles are retained; thus the stipulated surgery increases $N$ by exactly one. At stage $r$ of the supplied sequence, $N_r=N_0+r$, while the unchanged white trace still has exactly $M$ arcs. Applying step4.1 at that stage gives $r\leq M-N_0$. An infinite sequence would have a prefix of length $M-N_0+1$, contradicting this bound. This proves the finite termination assertion, including the empty sequence and the case $M=N_0$. The geometric hypotheses must hold at every stage; they have not been inferred from the names of any isotopy moves.

citations.quote: Assume countable choice. Let $S\subset S^3$ be the image of a smooth embedding of the standard $S^2$. There is a smooth ambient isotopy $H_t:S^3\to S^3$, with $H_0=\operatorname{id}$, such that $H_1(S)$ is the standard equatorial sphere $E$. In particular $S^3\setminus S$ has exactly two components. Their closures $B_+$ and $B_-$ are smoothly embedded standard closed $3$-balls with common boundary $S$. If $D_+$ and $D_-$ denote the standard closed hemispheres bounded by $E$, the labels can be chosen so that the restrictions $H_1:B_\pm\to D_\pm$ are diffeomorphisms with the same boundary restriction $H_1|_S:S\to E$. Thus the ball identifications are compatible on their boundary and on a common two-sided collar of that boundary.
An oriented link $L\subset S^3$ is **split** if a smoothly embedded sphere $S\subset S^3\setminus L$ has link points in both components of $S^3\setminus S$; otherwise $L$ is **nonsplit**.

Assume countable choice. For $n=2$ or $3$, a smoothly embedded closed $n$-ball in a connected boundaryless smooth $n$-manifold can be carried to a sufficiently small coordinate round ball by a smooth ambient isotopy. Consequently, a smooth closed disk in the boundary of a smooth $3$-ball is a standard disk window: the pair consisting of the ball and that disk is diffeomorphic to a round ball with a hemispherical boundary disk. Attaching a smooth $3$-ball to a smooth manifold along one such disk window does not change the diffeomorphism type, after smoothing the corner. The same conclusion holds in reverse, when a ball meeting the boundary in one disk is removed; the diffeomorphism is supported near the attached or removed ball and its attaching collar.

Let $P$ be a compact smooth $k$-manifold with boundary, let $N$ be a Hausdorff smooth $n$-manifold without boundary, and let $f:P\times[0,1]\to N$ be jointly smooth with every $f_t$ a smooth embedding. Suppose the family is stationary on neighborhoods of both time endpoints. For every open neighborhood $W$ of its compact track $f(P\times[0,1])$, there is a jointly smooth isotopy $H_t:N\to N$ of diffeomorphisms with $H_0=\operatorname{id}$ and $H_t\circ f_0=f_t$, supported in a fixed compact subset of $W$ and stationary near its time endpoints. No choice axiom is assumed. The empty source and zero-dimensional source are allowed.

Assume countable choice. Let $B$ be a supplied smooth closed $3$-ball and let $F\subset B$ be a compact neatly properly embedded smooth surface, possibly disconnected, with no closed components. If at least one component of $F$ is not a disk, there exists an embedded disk $X\subset\operatorname{int}B$ such that $X\cap F=\partial X$ and $\partial X$ does not bound a disk in $F$. The assertion concerns a geometric compressing disk for the whole surface; it does not require specifying its boundary component in advance.

derivations.claim: By geometric incompressibility, $c=\partial D$ bounds a disk $E$ in $F$. It lies in $\operatorname{int}F$, because $c$ is an interior regular circle and the disk it bounds is a subsurface disk. Since $c$ misses $G$, every component of $(F\cap G)\setminus L$ meeting $E$ would lie wholly in its interior: it cannot cross $c$. Such a component is a proper arc with endpoints on $L$, whereas $E$ misses $L$. Thus $E\cap G=\varnothing$. If the optional $N$ is supplied, each product boundary annulus of $F\cap N$ is connected, misses $c$, and meets $L$ outside $E$; hence it misses $E$ entirely. Thus $E$ misses $N$, as does the supplied $D$. Likewise, if $Q$ is supplied, $c$ misses $Q$; any connected component of $F\cap Q$ meeting $\operatorname{int}E$ would lie wholly inside $E$ and yet meet $L\cup G$, a contradiction. Thus $E$ and $D$ also miss $Q$. The disk $D$ also misses $G$ and $L$, so the sphere $E\cup D$, rounded along its corner, has a neighborhood disjoint from $G\cup L$ and, when supplied, $N$ and $Q$.

Carry out two-copy surgery: remove a narrow annulus about $c$ in $F$, cap its two sides by nearby copies of $D$, and round. One resulting component is the sphere $S_0$ obtained from $E\cup D$; the other part $F_1$ is $F$ with the disk replacement. The sphere and $F_1$ are disjoint, and $S_0$ misses $G\cup L$, by step1.1. This disk replacement leaves the component count and all boundary circles of $F$ unchanged, so each component of $F_1$ still meets $L$. By [F1], $S_0$ has a closed ball side $V$ with no link points. Every component of $F_1$, being disjoint from $S_0$ and having boundary outside $V$, lies outside $V$. Likewise every component of $G$ lies outside $V$, because it has nonempty boundary in $L$ and misses $S_0$. Every component of the optional tube $N$ contains a component of $L$ and misses $S_0$, so $N$ also lies outside $V$. Each supplied connected piece of $Q$ misses $S_0$ and meets $L\cup G$ outside $V$, so it too is outside $V$. Consequently the interior of $V$ contains neither $F_1$ nor $G$ nor the optional $N$ or $Q$.

Reverse the short surgery tube between $S_0$ and $F_1$. Absorb that tube's product collar into $V$, using [F2]. It gives a ball $V'$ meeting $F_1$ exactly in one disk window; its remaining boundary, with the window's edge rounded, is the old disk bulge. Its interior misses $F_1$, and the entire ball and its short attaching collar miss $L\cup G$ and the optional $N$ and $Q$. Choose the collars small enough to retain these disjointness properties. This is the actual empty ball needed for the replacement; no assertion that a homotopy disk may pass through the other surface is used.

In the standard window and collar parameters from [F2], make the cap thin by positive normal rescaling. The bulged disk is then $t=\gamma(x)$ over a planar disk, where $\gamma$ is smooth and vanishes on its outer collar; the window is $t=0$. The graphs $t=(1-u)\gamma(x)$ give a smooth embedding isotopy agreeing with the fixed rest of the surface on that collar. The ball interior contains no other surface, so these graphs remain disjoint from the unchanged part. Its track and a sufficiently small open neighborhood miss $L\cup G$ and the optional $N$ and $Q$. Apply [F3] with that neighborhood, obtaining the claimed ambient isotopy fixed there. Reversing the flattening if necessary carries the original $F$ to $F_1$. All auxiliary copies and roundings may be made arbitrarily close to the given $D$, and all changes outside $E$ are confined to an arbitrarily small collar of $c$. This proves the first assertion.

For the finite-ball assertion, $F\cap H_i$ is a compact neat proper surface after using its transverse boundary chart. It has no closed components: a closed component would be an open and closed component of the whole surface $F$, since it has no intersection with $\partial H_i$, contrary to the fact that every component of $F$ has boundary on $L$ outside $H_i$. If a nondisk component occurs, [F4] supplies a disk $D\subset\operatorname{int}H_i$ whose boundary $c$ is essential in $F\cap H_i$ and whose interior misses $F$. It also misses $G$, since the chamber interior does, and misses $N$ and $Q$ when those optional sets are supplied under their chamber-interior hypotheses. Its transverse collar may be chosen in the same chamber. Thus steps1.1–4.1 apply.

The disk $E\subset F$ from step1.1 cannot be contained in $H_i$: otherwise it would be contained in the component of $F\cap H_i$ containing $c$, contradicting the chosen essentiality. Since its boundary lies in $\operatorname{int}H_i$, it must cross $\partial H_i$. For every $j$, the boundary $c$ misses $\partial H_j$, because $c\subset\operatorname{int}H_i$ and distinct ball interiors are disjoint. Therefore every component of $F\cap\partial H_j$ meeting $E$ lies wholly inside $E$. Each such intersection is a complete circle, and at least one occurs for $j=i$. Choose the new disk and its attaching collar wholly in $\operatorname{int}H_i$, hence disjoint from every ball boundary. The replacement removes precisely those trace circles contained in $E$ and adds none. It leaves all other traces unchanged and retains transversality. Thus the finite integer $\sum_j |F\cap\partial H_j|$ strictly decreases.

Every replacement is an ambient isotopy fixed on $L\cup G$ and on the optional $N$ and $Q$ under their stated chamber-disjointness assumptions, so it preserves geometric incompressibility, the absence of closed components and the exact proper-arc intersection with $G$, and the components and incidences of $F\cap Q$ when supplied. Repeat step5.1 whenever a nondisk chamber piece remains. Step6.1 bounds the number of repetitions by the initial nonnegative trace count. At termination no nondisk piece remains; if one did, [F4] and the same construction would yield another strict decrease. Concatenate the finitely many smooth ambient isotopies, with stationary time ends. This proves simultaneous disk-piece normalization for the entire supplied family, including the empty family. It uses the actual rounded transverse ball data in the Statement and makes no claim that arbitrary unprepared corner data already satisfy them.

derivations.claim: The interior of $\alpha$ belongs to one component of $S\setminus\Gamma$, and faces one cut-ball $K$. Both ends face the same copy of $\Delta$ on $\partial K$. Indeed, $\gamma$ separates $S$ by [F1], so the chord approaches both ends from the same side of $\gamma$. Along the boundary of a proper disk the two sides of that circle correspond to its two disk faces: orient the disk and use its continuous normal to distinguish them. This identification is constant along $\gamma$, and the chosen component of $S\setminus\Gamma$ remains on one face. Using a smooth parameter of $\Delta$, join the chord endpoints by a proper embedded arc $\beta$ whose endpoint tangents are transverse to $\gamma$. On $\partial K$, the two arcs $\alpha$ and $\beta$ now form an embedded circle with two corners. It bounds a disk region $R$ by [F1]; use the supplied boundary-sphere chart and [F2] for its smooth corner parameter. Push the interior of $R$ into $K$ using its inward collar, keeping the boundary fixed and positive collar height at every interior point. This yields the disk $X$ with interior disjoint from all boundary faces, hence from $F$. It misses $G$, since its interior is in $\operatorname{int}H$ and its boundary lies in $\alpha\cup\beta$, also disjoint from $G$.

Here is a local smooth model for the strip push, including its two end neighborhoods. Parametrize the bigon $X$ so its edges are $r=0$ and $r=h(s)$ for $0\leq s\leq1$, where $h>0$ on $(0,1)$, $h(0)=h(1)=0$, and both endpoint zeros are simple. The first edge is $\beta$ and the second $\alpha$. The transverse end collars and [F2] extend this to coordinates $(s,t,r)$ on a thin neighborhood of $X$: $F$ is $r=0$ near $\beta$, and $S$ is $r=h(s)$ near $\alpha$. The two edge prescriptions are compatible at their transverse corners; in their two-dimensional tangent plane they are the two sides of the bigon, while $t$ is the transverse coordinate. Extend $h$ negatively just beyond its two simple zeros. Shrink the coordinate neighborhood so it contains no other sheet of $F$, and no other sheet of $S$ beyond that prescribed graph; compactness of the disk and injectivity of its collars permit this. A slight extension past $r=h(s)$ remains disjoint from the compact obstacle and $\partial F$. Choose a nonnegative smooth $q(s)$ supported in this extended interval, with $q(s)>h(s)$ on $[0,1]$, and so close to $h$ on the positive interval that its graph lies in the chosen slight extension. Choose an even smooth cutoff $\chi(t)$, equal to one on a smaller central strip, zero outside a slightly larger strip, and strictly decreasing between those two strips for $t>0$. Replace $F$ there by the graphs $r=u q(s)\chi(t)$, $0\leq u\leq1$. They agree with the fixed surface on the outside collars and remain embeddings because they are graphs in a neighborhood containing no other sheet. This is a smooth embedding isotopy of the entire surface, supported near the actual disk, and its track misses $G\cup\partial F$.

At the final time, the new intersection with $S$ satisfies $\chi(t)=h(s)/q(s)$. For $0<s<1$ the right side lies strictly between zero and one, so it gives exactly two arcs, on the two transition strips $t>0$ and $t<0$. Near either endpoint the implicit function theorem applies using the nonzero derivative of $h$ there, so each arc joins smoothly to the unchanged traces beyond the strip. These are exactly the two copies of $\alpha$ joining the cut ends of the two complementary paths of $\gamma$. They form two circles. In $H$, the strip along the proper arc $\beta$ has been removed from $\Delta$; the retained pieces are its two disk sides, with their rounded strip collars. Every other disk piece is unchanged. Thus the trace count increases by one and all the stated proper pieces remain disks. Make the graph family stationary at its time ends and apply [F3] in a neighborhood of its compact track disjoint from $G\cup\partial F$. This gives the asserted ambient isotopy with the required support and fixed sets.

In ZF, let $n\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open, let $f:U\to\mathbb R^n$ be smooth, and let $a\in U$. If $Df(a)$ is invertible, then there are open neighbourhoods $a\in V\subseteq U$ and $f(a)\in W$ such that $f|_V:V\to W$ is a diffeomorphism. Writing $g=(f|_V)^{-1}$,
$$Dg(y)=Df(g(y))^{-1}\qquad(y\in W).$$
No choice axiom is used.

Let $P$ be a compact smooth $k$-manifold with boundary, let $N$ be a Hausdorff smooth $n$-manifold without boundary, and let $f:P\times[0,1]\to N$ be jointly smooth with every $f_t$ a smooth embedding. Suppose the family is stationary on neighborhoods of both time endpoints. For every open neighborhood $W$ of its compact track $f(P\times[0,1])$, there is a jointly smooth isotopy $H_t:N\to N$ of diffeomorphisms with $H_0=\operatorname{id}$ and $H_t\circ f_0=f_t$, supported in a fixed compact subset of $W$ and stationary near its time endpoints. No choice axiom is assumed. The empty source and zero-dimensional source are allowed.

derivations.claim: Consider a common-axis book. The surface tangent plane contains the axis direction and is transverse to $W=\{y=0\}$, so the projection of that plane to the $(z,y)$ coordinates has rank two. By [F1], near each axis point $F$ is a graph $x=f(z,y)$ with $f(z,0)=0$. The supplied neat end collars give the same graph on a half-neighborhood at $z=\pm1$ and a small extension across it. Finitely many such charts cover the compact axis. Their graph functions agree on smaller overlaps, since they describe the same local embedded sheet containing the axis. Shrinking uniformly gives a single graph on $[-1,1]\times[-a,a]$. There are no other surface sheets in a sufficiently thin axis neighborhood: after removing smaller source neighborhoods of the axis, the remaining compact source image has a positive separation from it. Also $|f(z,y)|\leq A|y|$ for a finite derivative bound $A$, by the fundamental theorem of calculus.

Put $f_u(z,y)=(1-u)f(z,y)+u k y$, for $0\leq u\leq1$. On a thin neighborhood of its compact graph track take the time-dependent field $V_u=(k y-f(z,y))\partial_x$, multiplied by a smooth cutoff equal to one on the entire inner graph track and supported in a larger axis neighborhood. The cutoff can be constant through the end caps and extended across their product collars. The field has no $z$ component, so it is tangent to both end caps; it is zero on $W$, because $f(z,0)=0$, and is zero near the lateral boundary. The derivative bound in step1.1 makes the entire graph track lie in the chosen larger neighborhood for sufficiently small $|y|$. Its velocity is exactly $V_u$ there. By uniqueness in [F2] the field evolution carries that graph to $x=f_u(z,y)$ and fixes the axis and $W$ pointwise. The rest of the surface is transported by the same ambient diffeomorphisms. Shrinking the final inner radius further excludes the transported compact complement, whose image is disjoint from the fixed axis. Thus the final intersection with that inner book is exactly $x=k y$.

In a transverse-axis book, list its finitely many intersection heights $z_j$. At each such point, projection of $F$ to $(x,y)$ has rank two, so [F1] gives a graph $z=h_j(x,y)$ with $h_j(0,0)=z_j$. Use disjoint height neighborhoods for these finitely many graphs. Compactness excludes all other sheets from a smaller axis neighborhood, as in step1.1. For each graph use $h_{j,u}=(1-u)h_j+u z_j$ and the field $(z_j-h_j(x,y))\partial_z$, with a cutoff equal to one on its inner graph track and supported in its height neighborhood and a small radial disk. These supports miss the end caps and the lateral boundary. Each field vanishes on the axis, and is tangent to $W$, since it has only a $z$ component. Its evolution from [F2] therefore fixes the axis pointwise and preserves $W$ setwise. Uniqueness carries the inner graph to $z=h_{j,u}$. The finitely many disjointly supported evolutions leave exactly the flat section disks $z=z_j$ in a sufficiently thin final book; exclude the transported compact source complement exactly as in step2.1.

All the fields are tangent to the supplied cap boundaries or vanish near them, and vanish near the lateral boundaries, so their evolutions restrict to book diffeomorphisms. The product collar extensions paste them to an ambient isotopy outside the books; extend the fields by zero beyond those collar neighborhoods. The finite disjoint supports permit concatenation, and a smooth time reparametrization makes all stages stationary at their ends. This preserves the fixed axes, the set $W$ and the asserted boundary behavior. No new surface pieces can enter the thin final books, by the compact-complement separation already proved.

A flat section disk intersects the lateral circle in its entire circumference. The axes $x=0$ and $y=0$ mark four successive corner points; between them are alternately two $xy<0$ and two $xy>0$ arcs. Its two page diameters cut it into four disk quadrants. In a common-axis band $x=k y$, $k>0$ gives $xy=k y^2>0$ on each lateral edge, so it misses the $C_+$ strips. Both pages cut this band along the single common axis, leaving two rectangular disks. These are literal coordinate computations, so they persist under the actual supplied book maps. Together with steps2.1–4.1 they give all the claimed normal forms, without an additional choice or a global gluing assumption.
